body_markdown:
A shopper asking ChatGPT which running shoes work for flat feet is not searching for a brand. They are waiting for one to be recommended to them. Before they reach any product page, an AI system has already compared options, surfaced a shortlist, and in some cases, closed the decision entirely.


Nearly[3 in 4](https://www.morningstar.com/news/business-wire/20251020127097/global-study-73-of-shoppers-using-ai-in-shopping-journey-but-merchants-face-new-agentic-commerce-risks) shoppers are already using AI as part of their shopping journey.


Previously, SEO, paid media and sponsored deals enabled a degree of owned and earned media control. That control has moved. Brands now have minimal direct input into the initial consumer decision-making process.


For retailers, this raises a question most haven’t fully confronted. When AI mediates the purchase journey, who controls the outcome? Either you own the AI experience, or you become inventory. The brands that understand this distinction are building now.


## What “AI-Mediated Commerce” Actually Means


“AI-mediated commerce” describes what happens when a third-party AI platform (e.g. ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini) enters the customer journey before the shopper has decided where to buy. The platform compares products across brands, generates recommendations, and often closes the decision before the customer has visited any brand’s owned channel.


This is meaningfully different from conversational AI deployed on a brand’s own website or app, where the brand controls the experience, the product data surfaced, and the conversational flow that leads to purchase. In AI-mediated commerce, the intermediary is a third party’s system, working from whatever product data it can access. The brand’s influence on that interaction is indirect, routed entirely through the quality and structure of its catalog data.


That distinction matters because it relocates the control point. Brands are used to owning the conversation once a shopper arrives on their properties. In AI-mediated discovery, that conversation happens somewhere else, and the brand either shows up accurately or it doesn’t.


This shift to AI mediation is a byproduct of the overall industry transition from Search Commerce to Conversational Commerce to Agentic Commerce.


## What Actually Changes in the Journey


To understand the practical stakes, it helps to map what shifts when AI steps into the purchase journey.


**Journey Stage** **Traditional Journey** **AI-Mediated Journey**


Discovery Shopper searches Google or visits a brand site directly Shopper asks an AI assistant for a recommendation


Comparison Shopper browses several brand sites AI compares options across the web based on available product data


Decision Shopper reviews product pages and reads reviews AI synthesizes information and surfaces one or two options


Purchase Shopper navigates to checkout on a brand’s site Shopper is directed to one brand, or purchases within the AI interface


In a traditional journey, brands have multiple touchpoints to shape the experience, correct misimpressions, and guide a shopper toward purchase. In an AI-mediated journey, those touchpoints compress toward a singular point, i.e. the moment the AI reads your product data.


### The integrity of catalog infrastructure is more important than ever


If your data is out of date, misattributed or difficult to parse, erroneous information is likely to be regurgitated back to the consumer. A shopper may be told a product is out of stock when inventory exists or a size range may be described inaccurately. Competitors will be surfaced over your brand because the AI found a cleaner match elsewhere.


These are failures that happen upstream of a brand’s owned channel, often without any signal that the conversion never came.


## Three Risks Worth Taking Seriously


Brands tend to focus on discoverability as the primary concern in AI-mediated commerce. That’s valid, but it’s one part of a larger picture.


**Risk** **What Happens**


Invisibility Products don’t appear in AI-generated results. Organic discovery flows to brands whose data is better structured and more readable to AI systems.


Misrepresentation Products appear with inaccurate attributes, outdated pricing, or incomplete variants. The shopper’s first impression is set before they’ve engaged with the brand directly.


Disintermediation Even when visible and accurately represented, the customer relationship belongs to the AI platform. First-party data, direct communication, and the ability to build loyalty all follow the relationship.


The compounding effect across all three makes a compelling case for taking the infrastructure question seriously now, not in the next planning cycle.


Consumer reliance on AI agents and LLMs is already becoming embedded. If your data is misrepresented or, worse still, missing entirely, this will have a profound effect on sales.


Brands are already seeing how this plays out in their own web analytics. Organic traffic has declined[15–25%](https://www.bain.com/insights/goodbye-clicks-hello-ai-zero-click-search-redefines-marketing/) for retailers as “zero-click” behavior (where entire fact-finding missions or purchase journeys take place within a chat window or AI search result) becomes standard.


## The Infrastructure Question Brands Should Be Asking


Most discussion around AI-mediated commerce focuses on the AI systems doing the mediating. Which models are generating recommendations? What are their capabilities and how do they rank options? This is the wrong starting point for a brand.


The more useful question is **“what does an AI system need in order to represent my products accurately?”**


The answer is structured, machine-readable product data. Clean and complete taxonomies with standardized attributes, and accurate pricing and inventory signals. Product descriptions and specifications that AI systems can parse without ambiguity. Schema markup and structured metadata that indicate to AI platforms how a product should be categorized, what it’s suited for, and how it compares to alternatives.


Many retailers carry catalogs with attributes inconsistently labeled across product lines, variants missing for certain SKUs, category naming that varies by region or team. For a human browsing a site, these gaps are manageable, but for an AI building a recommendation across thousands of products, they’re the difference between being included in the answer and being absent from it.


Accurate data solves one half of the problem. The other half is what the AI is permitted to do with it. Even a system reading perfect product data can still improvise a discount, misstate a return policy, or make a claim your brand never approved. This is not something prompt engineering can solve. Policy compliance has to be a system constraint built into how the AI reasons and acts, not an instruction layered on afterward. A model that can be prompted into non-compliance becomes a liability. Simply put, it needs to be a governed system.


The good news is, all of these goals can be realized. With the right infrastructure, automated catalog enrichment, taxonomy normalization, and discoverability optimization are all quickly achievable capabilities.


## Where Brand Control Actually Lives


The shift to AI-mediated commerce doesn’t eliminate brand control. It relocates it.


A recent investigation found that in retail,[48%](https://www.yext.com/research/article/ai-citations-user-locations-query-context#differences-by-industry) of AI citations come from brand-managed websites. Another 38% came from third-party listings sites and aggregators, which are largely pulling data from brand feeds and assets.


Retailers that invest in clean, enriched, structured product data create the conditions for accurate AI representation wherever the shopper starts. Those that publish schema-marked data in formats AI systems can ingest extend their reach beyond their own channels. And brands that build strong AI commerce execution on their own properties retain full control over the experience when the journey does arrive with them.


These strategies work together. A brand that prepares its catalog for external AI discoverability, runs effective conversational AI on its own site, and operates frictionless checkout is building a position that holds across both human-led and AI-mediated journeys. The brands doing all three have a meaningful head start over those still treating these as separate problems.


## Retailers Can Take Back Control in an AI-Mediated World


AI-mediated commerce is not a future scenario to plan for. It’s a present condition to adapt to.


Shoppers are already making decisions upstream of brand-owned channels, and the gap between brands with structured data infrastructure and those without is widening. That gap shows up in organic traffic, in conversion rates, and in the first-party customer relationships that don’t form because the AI never directed the shopper to you in the first place.


The brands that retain control in this environment are the ones that understand where the control point has moved to, and build for it.
